claim: Many mRNA attributes can affect the speed of the translating ribosome, including secondary structure.
source: Many mRNA attributes can affect the speed of the translating ribosome, including secondary structure (Doma and Parker, 2006), nucleotide and codon composition (Chaney and Clark, 2015; Gardin et al., 2014; Letzring et al., 2010; Forrest et al., 2020; Hia et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Narula et al., 2019), tRNA abundance (Ishimura et al., 2014; Novoa and Ribas de Pouplana, 2012; Nakahigashi et al., 2014), the sequence of the nascent peptide and its interaction with the ribosome exit tunnel or other ribosome-associated factors (Brandman et al., 2012; Charneski and Hurst, 2013; Kuroha et al., 2010; Tanner et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2020; Buschauer et al., 2020; Absmeier et al., 2023), and damage or improper processing of the mRNA itself (Brandman and Hegde, 2016; Joazeiro, 2019; Simms et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Stalling sequences are specific mRNA sequences that can cause the ribosome to pause or stall during translation.

claim: Codon usage bias affects translation elongation rates and protein synthesis efficiency.

claim: Rare codon usage influences protein folding dynamics.

claim: Recognition of slow ribosome dynamics by the mRNA decay machinery can trigger mRNA degradation during ribosome-associated quality control (RQC).

evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: General mRNA decay in eukaryotes is initiated by shortening of the poly(A) tail mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex with its catalytic subunits CNOT7 and CNOT8.
source: In eukaryotes, general mRNA decay is initiated by a shortening of the poly(A) tail mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex with its catalytic subunits CNOT7 and CNOT8, followed by 5′-to-3′ mRNA decay, where the mRNA is decapped by the DCP1/DCP2 decapping complex and then exonucleolytically degraded by the exonuclease XRN1 (Mugridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: After deadenylation, 5′-to-3′ mRNA decay occurs where the mRNA is decapped by the DCP1/DCP2 decapping complex and then exonucleolytically degraded by the exonuclease XRN1.
source: In eukaryotes, general mRNA decay is initiated by a shortening of the poly(A) tail mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex with its catalytic subunits CNOT7 and CNOT8, followed by 5′-to-3′ mRNA decay, where the mRNA is decapped by the DCP1/DCP2 decapping complex and then exonucleolytically degraded by the exonuclease XRN1 (Mugridge et al., 2018).

claim: A reporter construct was created containing a Renilla luciferase open reading frame where the final 30 codons were replaced by synonymous but rarely used codons.

evidence: Experimental design described in the text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Introducing the rare codon stretch into the Renilla luciferase open reading frame significantly reduced the half-life of the translated mRNA from >10 hr to 8.0±4.4 hr.
source: As expected, introducing the rare codon stretch into the Renilla luciferase open reading frame significantly reduced the half-life of the translated mRNA from >10 hr to 8.0±4.4 hr (Figure 1B and C).

claim: Codon composition directly affects mRNA stability in human cells.

evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data and supported by citations to prior research

claim: HEK293T DDX6 KO cells were created using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing.

claim: Loss of DDX6 protein expression was verified by western blotting and sequencing of the genomic target site.
source: Loss of DDX6 protein expression was verified by western blotting and sequencing of the genomic target site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: The loss of DDX6 significantly stabilized the non-optimal codon-containing reporter, resulting in a measured half-life comparable to that of the respective control reporter (>10 hr vs 8.0±4.4 hr).

claim: The CCR4-NOT complex interacts with the empty ribosome E-site in both yeast and humans.

claim: Knockout of DDX6 does not affect the deadenylation activity of the CCR4-NOT complex.

claim: DDX6 participates in the mRNA decay process triggered by a slowed ribosome through a mechanism different from modulating CCR4-NOT activity.

claim: Yeast Dhh1p has been found to co-purify with ribosomal components.

claim: The ability of DDX6 orthologs to associate with ribosomes is a conserved feature across different species.

claim: The RecA2 domain of DDX6 mediates interactions with EDC3, LSM14A, PATL1, 4E-T, and GIGYF1/2 through their Phe-Asp-Phe (FDF) motifs in a mutually exclusive manner.
source: In addition to providing a link to the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, the RecA2 domain of DDX6 also mediates interactions with other regulatory proteins e.g., EDC3, LSM14A, PATL1, 4E-T, and GIGYF1/2. These proteins interact with DDX6 RecA2 through their Phe-Asp-Phe (FDF) motifs in a mutually exclusive manner, thereby either facilitating mRNA decay by linking the deadenylation machinery to the core decapping complex or inducing translational repression (Fromm et al., 2012; Tritschler et al., 2008; Nissan et al., 2010; Sharif et al., 2013; Tritschler et al., 2009; Brandmann et al., 2018; Ozgur et al., 2015a; Peter et al., 2019).

evidence: Explanation of how ribosome profiling data is interpreted

claim: Ribosome footprints tend to accumulate at sites with reduced ribosome speed.
source: In particular, ribosome footprints tend to accumulate at sites with reduced ribosome speed (Ingolia et al., 2011) and can, therefore, be used to study ribosome pausing or stalling (Li et al., 2012; Guydosh and Green, 2014; Gamble et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Comparison of the RNA-seq datasets revealed 1707 mRNAs specifically upregulated in the absence of DDX6 (FDR <0.005).
source: Comparison of the RNA-seq datasets revealed 1707 mRNAs specifically upregulated in the absence of DDX6 (FDR <0.005; Figure 3A and C).
evidence: Primary finding from RNA-seq experiments shown in Figure 3A and C

claim: Of the 1707 upregulated mRNAs in DDX6 KO cells, 298 transcripts were upregulated more than twofold (logFC >1).
source: Of those, 298 transcripts were upregulated more than twofold (logFC >1).
evidence: Primary finding from RNA-seq experiments

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment for transcripts coding for proteins that localize in the extracellular space, to membranes or are involved in signaling or cell adhesion among upregulated mRNAs in DDX6 KO cells.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment for transcripts coding for proteins that localize in the extracellular space, to membranes or are involved in signaling or cell adhesion (Figure 3E).
evidence: Primary finding from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: 1484 transcripts were significantly downregulated in DDX6 KO cells (FDR <0.005).
source: On the other hand, 1484 transcripts were significantly downregulated (FDR <0.005; Figure 3A and C), 156 more than twofold (logFC < –1).
evidence: Primary finding from RNA-seq experiments shown in Figure 3A and C

claim: 260 transcripts were translationally upregulated in DDX6 KO cells (FDR <0.005).
source: Remarkably, 260 transcripts were translationally upregulated in DDX6 KO cells (FDR <0.005; Figure 3B and D), 152 more than twofold (logFC >1).
evidence: Primary finding from ribosome profiling and RNA-seq comparison shown in Figure 3B and D

claim: 89 of the 260 translationally upregulated genes in DDX6 KO cells encode zinc finger transcription factors (34%; FDR = 2.5E-46).
source: Functional characterization of these target genes revealed a strong predominance of genes encoding zinc finger transcription factors (89 of the 260 translationally upregulated genes; 34%; FDR = 2.5E-46) (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: Primary finding from functional characterization shown in Figure 3B and D

claim: GO-analysis showed an enrichment for DNA binding proteins and factors involved in transcription among translationally upregulated mRNAs in DDX6 KO cells.
source: Accordingly, GO-analysis showed an enrichment for DNA binding proteins and factors involved in transcription (Figure 3F).
evidence: Primary finding from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Only 38 transcripts showed significant downregulation in TE in DDX6 KO cells (FDR <0.005).
source: In contrast, only 38 transcripts showed significant downregulation in TE (FDR <0.005; Figure 3B and D), 17 more than twofold (logFC < –1), with no functional association as measured by GO analysis.
evidence: Primary finding from ribosome profiling and RNA-seq comparison shown in Figure 3B and D

claim: The 260 mRNAs translationally upregulated in DDX6 KO cells have significantly lower coding sequence (CDS) GC content than the rest of the mRNAs expressed in the same cells.
source: Comparison of the 260 upregulated mRNAs in DDX6 KO cells revealed that these mRNAs have significantly lower coding sequence (CDS) GC content than the rest of the mRNAs expressed in the same cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Primary finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: DDX6-regulated CDSes appear to be longer than unaffected mRNA CDSes.
source: Furthermore, DDX6-regulated CDSes appear to be longer than unaffected mRNA CDSes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Primary finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: In mammals, low codon GC content is correlated with low codon optimality.
source: Interestingly, in mammals, low codon GC content is correlated with low codon optimality (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: mRNAs translationally regulated by DDX6 (TE up in DDX6 KO cells) are associated with a substantially lower predicted mRNA stability score.
source: To this end we compared DDX6 translationally regulated mRNAs with a transcriptome-wide prediction analysis of mRNA stabilities based on the codon composition (Diez et al., 2022) and found that mRNAs translationally regulated by DDX6 (TE up in DDX6 KO cells) are associated with a substantially lower predicted mRNA stability score (Figure 3G).
evidence: Primary finding from comparison with predicted stability scores shown in Figure 3G

claim: mRNAs encoding zinc finger transcription factors collectively show a lower stability score than the average transcriptome.
source: In agreement with our data that many transcripts with increased TE in DDX6 KO cells encode zinc finger transcription factors, Diez et al. also report that mRNAs encoding zinc finger transcription factors collectively show a lower stability score than the average transcriptome.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and agreement with current findings

claim: DDX6 translationally regulates a specific group of mRNAs with low codon optimality and, therefore, low stability.
source: These findings suggest that DDX6 translationally regulates a specific group of mRNAs with low codon optimality and, therefore, low stability.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including GC content, predicted stability, and functional enrichment

claim: DDX6-regulated mRNAs were not found to have a significantly lower TE than the other mRNAs expressed in the cells.
source: Interestingly, DDX6-regulated mRNAs were not found to have a significantly lower TE than the other mRNAs expressed in the cells; however, loss of DDX6 significantly increased the TE of this subset of mRNAs above the overall TE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Primary finding from translation efficiency analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Loss of DDX6 significantly increased the TE of DDX6-regulated mRNAs above the overall TE.
source: Interestingly, DDX6-regulated mRNAs were not found to have a significantly lower TE than the other mRNAs expressed in the cells; however, loss of DDX6 significantly increased the TE of this subset of mRNAs above the overall TE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Primary finding from translation efficiency analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: 35 genes were identified that matched the criteria of being upregulated in DDX6 KO cells (logFC >1, FDR <0.005) and showing local increase of ribosome footprints.
source: We manually screened the list of transcripts with logFC >1 and a statistically significant change (FDR <0.005) in the RNA-seq experiment (298 transcripts) for the presence of a local increase of ribosome footprints as measured by the coupled ribosome profiling experiment and found 35 genes that matched these criteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–G and Material and methods).
evidence: Primary finding from manual screening of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–G

claim: The androgen receptor (AR) transcript containing CAG repeats is one of the most highly upregulated mRNAs in DDX6 KO cells.
source: It is worth mentioning that one of the most highly upregulated mRNAs in DDX6 KO cells is the androgen receptor (AR) transcript containing CAG repeats, coding for a stretch of glutamine repeats (poly Q).
evidence: Primary finding from RNA-seq data

claim: CAG expansions can cause altered elongation kinetics that can lead to CAG expansion diseases like Huntington's disease.
source: However, it is interesting to note that a recent preprint suggests that CAG expansions can cause altered elongation kinetics that can lead to CAG expansion diseases like Huntington's disease (Aviner et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to a preprint

claim: Repetitive codon sequences potentially lead to ribosome stalling because of limited tRNA availability.
source: Repetitive codon sequences potentially lead to ribosome stalling because of limited tRNA availability (Dana and Tuller, 2014; Ishimura et al., 2014; Novoa and Ribas de Pouplana, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DDX6 dependency was detected in 6 of the 9 tested mRNAs (AR, BMP2, LGALS1, DLX5, ENO2, PSMB9) by qPCR.
source: DDX6 dependency was detected in 6 of the 9 tested mRNAs (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A AR, BMP2, LGALS1, DLX5, ENO2, PSMB9; see also changes in mRNA abundance as determined by RNA-seq; note that especially for AR and ENO2 the changes in mRNA abundance appear to be underestimated by the qPCR analysis compared to the RNA-seq quantification which can possibly arise due to differences in normalization strategies of the different technologies or exact sample status).
evidence: Primary finding from qPCR validation shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A

claim: DDX6 KO cells had higher levels of target mRNAs compared to WT HEK293T cells, and were partially restored back to WT levels by expressing exogenous DDX6.
source: We observed that DDX6 KO cells had higher levels of target mRNAs compared to WT HEK293T cells, as also measured by the RNA-seq experiments, and were partially restored back to WT levels by expressing exogenous DDX6.
evidence: Primary finding from qPCR rescue experiments

claim: None of the mutant forms of DDX6 were able to restore target mRNA levels.
source: It should be noted that none of the mutant forms of DDX6 were able to restore target mRNA levels, consistent with the previous reporter experiments.
evidence: Primary finding from qPCR rescue experiments

claim: DDX6 plays a direct role in the regulation of target mRNA levels in HEK293T cells.
source: These results strongly suggest that DDX6 plays a direct role in the regulation of target mRNA levels in HEK293T cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from qPCR validation and rescue experiments

claim: Reporter constructs were created in which the putative ribosomal stalling region (RSR) was inserted downstream of the Renilla luciferase open reading frame, either preceding or following a stop-codon.
source: To test whether the identified translational pause sites in some of the endogenous DDX6-targeted mRNAs contribute to mRNA destabilization, we created different reporter constructs in which the putative ribosomal stalling region (RSR) was inserted downstream of the Renilla luciferase open reading frame, either preceding or following a stop-codon; R-LUC-RSR and R-LUC-stop-RSR, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental design described in the text and shown in Figure 4A

claim: The presence of the AR stalling sequence before the stop-codon strongly reduced the mRNA half-life compared to the control mRNA where the stop-codon precedes the stalling sequence.
source: As expected, the presence of the AR stalling sequence before the stop-codon strongly reduced the mRNA half-life compared to the control mRNA where the stop-codon precedes the stalling sequence (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: The presence of the BMP2 stalling sequence was associated with a strong translation-dependent reduction in mRNA half-life (4.0±1.9 hr compared to >10 hr in the control vector).
source: The same was true for the BMP2 stalling sequence: the presence of the stalling sequence was associated with a strong translation-dependent reduction in mRNA half-life (4.0±1.9 hr compared to >10 hr in the control vector) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: In HEK293T DDX6 KO cells, the R-LUC-stop and R-LUC constructs for both AR and BMP2 stalling sequences had similar half-lives.
source: To test whether the observed reduction in reporter mRNA stability containing endogenous ribosomal stalling sites was dependent on DDX6, we also performed the half-life measurements in HEK293T DDX6 KO cells, and observed that the R-LUC-stop and R-LUC constructs for both AR and BMP2 stalling sequences had similar half-lives (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4B–E

claim: DDX6 is required to trigger the co-translational mRNA decay induced by AR and BMP2 stalling sequences.
source: These results, therefore, confirm that DDX6 is required to trigger the co-translational mRNA decay induced by these sequences.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from reporter experiments in WT and DDX6 KO cells

claim: The reporters with the AR or BMP2 stalling sequences pulled down increased amounts of HA-RPL22 indicative of increased ribosome occupancy on these reporters.
source: In keeping with the mRNA half-life results, the reporters with the AR or BMP2 stalling sequences pulled down increased amounts of HA-RPL22 indicative of increased ribosome occupancy on these reporters (Figure 4F).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4F

claim: The inefficiency of translation modulates mRNA stability in human cells, aligning with findings in yeast.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that the inefficiency of translation modulates mRNA stability in human cells, aligning with findings in yeast.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings and comparison with yeast studies

claim: DDX6 plays an important role in triggering the decay of slowly translated mRNAs.
source: Moreover, DDX6 (the human ortholog of Dhh1p) plays an important role in triggering the decay of slowly translated mRNAs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings

claim: DDX6 is necessary to trigger the decay of sub-optimally translated mRNAs.
source: To investigate whether DDX6 is necessary to trigger the decay of sub-optimally translated mRNAs, we created a reporter construct containing a Renilla luciferase open reading frame where the last 30 codons were replaced by synonymous but rarely used codons, chosen to reduce the translation rate without altering the amino acid sequence.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from reporter experiments

claim: DDX6 serves as a mediator of ribosome stalling and mRNA decay, and this role is evolutionarily conserved from yeast to mammals.
source: This result illustrated that DDX6 serves as a mediator of ribosome stalling and mRNA decay, and this role is evolutionarily conserved from yeast to mammals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings and comparison with yeast studies

claim: DDX6-CCR4-NOT interactions are essential for ribosome stalling-dependent mRNA decay.
source: By overexpressing DDX6 mutants in DDX6 KO cells, we showed that DDX6-CCR4-NOT interactions are essential for ribosome stalling-dependent mRNA decay.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mutant analysis experiments

claim: Reporter mRNAs containing the ribosomal stalling region were only destabilized in the presence of both translation and DDX6.
source: Importantly, we also found that reporter mRNAs containing the ribosomal stalling region were only destabilized in the presence of both translation and DDX6.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from reporter experiments with stalling sequences

claim: Loss of DDX6 could disrupt co-translational proteostasis of factors associated with neurodegenerative diseases, leading to the characteristic formation of intracellular aggregates.
source: These findings suggest that loss of DDX6 could disrupt co-translational proteostasis of factors associated with neurodegenerative diseases, leading to the characteristic formation of intracellular aggregates.
evidence: Speculation based on the finding that DDX6 targets mRNAs with CAG repeats

claim: The human RNA helicase DDX6 plays a critical role in mediating translation efficiency and mRNA stability in human cells.
source: Together, our study establishes that the human RNA helicase DDX6 plays a critical role in mediating translation efficiency and mRNA stability in human cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the collective experimental findings in the study
